Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Acute, intensely pruritic, dry/cracked erythematous rash on chest, hands, inner elbows.  
• Past eczema; no systemic symptoms; minimal response to OTC topical steroid/antihistamine.

Working diagnosis  
• Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare – highly likely given history, flexural involvement, dry cracked skin, and pruritus.

Considerations (plausible alternatives)  
• Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis – acute onset, new distribution; monitor for product triggers.  
• Scabies infestation – less likely but consider if no improvement or if flat-mates develop itch.

Management  
• Prescribe higher-potency topical corticosteroid (specific agent/strength not documented).  
• Prescribe emollient for bath/shower and frequent moisturising.  
• Prescribe oral non-sedating antihistamine (Fexofenadine) – dose/frequency not documented.  
• Advise diary of potential triggers (detergents, clothing, soaps).  
• Review in 1 week; earlier if worsening.  
• If poor response, consider dermatology referral and/or skin scraping for scabies (consideration only).

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  
  • Educated on skin care with emollients, avoidance of irritants; no broader chronic disease counselling recorded.

- Patient health goals and priorities:  Relief of itch and return to normal sleep/work.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare – High likelihood: prior eczema, flexural involvement, dry cracked skin, intense pruritus, no systemic illness.  
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – Medium likelihood: acute onset, chest & hand distribution, possible unrecognized exposure.  
3. Scabies infestation – Low-medium likelihood: severe itch, hand involvement, shared housing; no burrows noted.
